questions.q: A test's **sensitivity** is 99%. Which conditional probability is that?
options: P(positive test | sick)
P(sick | positive test)
P(sick)
P(positive test | healthy)
questions.why: Sensitivity is the chance the test is positive when the person really is sick, a likelihood. P(sick | positive) is the posterior, which is what patients care about and what Bayes' theorem calculates. Confusing the two is the classic error.

questions.q: The same screening test is used in two populations: in one 1% of people have the disease, in the other 20%. Where is a positive result more worrying?
options: In the 20% population, because a higher base rate means a larger share of positives are true cases
In the 1% population, because the disease is rarer
Equally worrying, because the test is identical
It cannot be compared without knowing the sample size
questions.why: With sensitivity 99% and a 5% false-positive rate, P(sick | positive) is about 17% at a 1% base rate but about 83% at 20%. The test is the same; only the prior changed. Ignoring this is the base-rate fallacy.

questions.q: Out of 10,000 people, 2% have a condition. The test catches 90% of cases and gives false positives for 10% of healthy people. What is P(condition | positive)?
options: About 18%
About 15.5%
questions.why: 200 sick → 180 true positives. 9,800 healthy → 980 false positives. P = 180 / (180 + 980) = 180 / 1,160 ≈ 15.5%. 90% is the sensitivity, P(positive | condition); 18% divides 180 by 1,000 instead of by all positives.

questions.q: Plant A makes 60% of parts with a 1% defect rate; plant B makes 40% with a 3% defect rate. A defective part is returned. What is the probability it came from plant B?
options: About 67%
questions.why: Prior × likelihood: A 0.60 × 0.01 = 0.006, B 0.40 × 0.03 = 0.012. Total 0.018. P(B | defective) = 0.012 / 0.018 ≈ 67%. 40% is the prior, ignoring the evidence; 75% compares defect rates alone (3 / (1 + 3)), ignoring the prior.

questions.q: A card issuer's fraud model gives P(fraud | alert) = 8.7%. What does this imply for operations?
options: The model is useless and should be switched off
Every alert should block the card, since fraud is costly
91.3% of fraud is missed by the model
More than 9 in 10 alerts are honest customers, so a light first response (such as an SMS confirmation) beats blocking the card, and the investigation team must be sized for all alerts
questions.why: A low posterior is the natural result of a rare event (0.2% of payments). The model still raises the fraud probability from 0.2% to 8.7%, more than 40-fold. 91.3% describes false alarms among alerts, not missed fraud; the model actually catches 95% of fraud.

questions.q: After one positive result, P(condition) = 15.5% (sensitivity 90%, false-positive rate 10%). A second, independent test with the same accuracy is also positive. What is the updated probability?
options: About 31%
About 90%
About 62%
About 15.5%, because the test is the same
questions.why: Yesterday's posterior becomes today's prior: 0.9 × 0.155 = 0.140; 0.1 × 0.845 = 0.085; posterior = 0.140 / (0.140 + 0.085) ≈ 62%. Doubling to 31% is not how evidence combines; 90% is the sensitivity again.

questions.q: The two-test calculation assumes the tests are **independent**. If a false positive on the first test makes a false positive on the second more likely (for example, the same cross-reacting substance), what happens?
options: Nothing; the posterior is unchanged
The calculated posterior is too high: correlated errors make the second positive less informative than assumed
The calculated posterior is too low
The prior must be reset to the base rate
questions.why: Bayesian updating multiplies in the second likelihood ratio only if the evidence is conditionally independent. If errors are correlated, the second positive adds less information and the true posterior is lower. The same "naive" independence assumption underlies Naive Bayes classifiers.

questions.q: In an interview: "Most of our fraud alerts are false. A vendor offers a model that catches 99% of fraud instead of our 95%, with the same 2% false-alarm rate on honest payments (fraud base rate 0.2%). Will it fix the problem?"
options: Yes, a 99% detection rate will make most alerts real
Barely: P(fraud | alert) rises only from about 8.7% to about 9.0%; with a rare event, cutting the false-positive rate matters far more
Yes, it will halve the false alerts
No, because detection rate has no effect on the posterior
questions.why: Out of 1,00,000 payments: 198 true alerts versus 1,996 false ones, so 198 / 2,194 ≈ 9.0%. The false alerts come from the huge pool of honest payments, so the false-positive rate dominates. Detection rate does affect the posterior, just very little here.
